strengths: Strong empirical motivation: Section 2 provides clear, well-visualized evidence for diverse attention patterns (global/positional/semantic-dependent) and demonstrates that low-entropy tokens suffer disproportionately from KV eviction, directly motivating the reward design used later.

The two-stage training pipeline (supervised distillation from a 'Golden Eviction' oracle followed by GRPO-based RL formulated as an MDP) is a sensible and reasonably novel way to address the dynamic, non-stationary nature of KV importance that prior rule-based or one-shot trained methods miss.

Extensive experimental validation across multiple model families (Qwen3-4B/1.7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, MiniCPM-4.1-8B) and benchmarks (AIME2024/2025, GPQA, LiveCodeBench), with comparisons against a wide range of baselines (H2O, SnapKV, R-KV, RPC, G-KV, DuoAttention), consistently showing favorable results at reduced budgets.
Useful ablations isolating the contributions of the reward design, input features, and sampling strategy, which support several of the design choices rather than treating them as arbitrary.
Efficiency analysis (throughput, concurrent batch size, end-to-end speed, and overhead of the scoring model itself) substantiates the practical value of the method beyond accuracy numbers alone.

An accompanying theoretical bound (Appendix A) attempts to formally justify why minimizing evicted attention mass reduces approximation error, adding some rigor to the intuition behind Golden Eviction.
weaknesses: The theoretical result in Appendix A only bounds single-step approximation error as a function of instantaneous evicted attention mass; it does not justify the multi-step 'max over future blocks' criterion that Golden Eviction actually uses, creating a gap between the stated theoretical motivation and the proposed algorithm's long-term/future-looking design.

The overhead of generating Golden Eviction supervision (full T×T attention matrices per training sequence) and of training/storing separate scoring models per layer and attention-head group is not clearly quantified, raising reproducibility and scalability concerns, especially since a new scoring model apparently must be trained per base LLM.

Memory/latency overhead of the additional attention-feature vectors and KV concatenation used as scoring-model input is not clearly accounted for against the claimed memory savings; the paper reports scoring-model runtime overhead but not its footprint relative to the compressed cache itself.

Generalization claims are tested only on other reasoning-style benchmarks (GPQA, LiveCodeBench) despite the entropy-based motivation in Section 2.2 explicitly using summarization data; broader domain transfer (e.g., long-document QA, summarization) is not evaluated even though it was used to motivate the method.

AIME2024/2025 contain only ~30 problems each; despite 32 repeated runs, no variance/confidence intervals are reported in the main results (Figure 3), making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported gains, particularly at the smallest budgets where curves are close together.

Baseline hyperparameters (e.g., R-KV's fixed 0.1/0.9 weighting) are taken directly from prior work without apparent re-tuning for the reasoning-model long-generation setting used here, raising some concern about comparison fairness.

The Impact Statement is boilerplate and the paper lacks an explicit, dedicated limitations discussion (e.g., training cost, per-model retraining requirement, oracle-vs-online distribution shift), which would strengthen transparency given the added system complexity introduced by the trained scoring models.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem (KV cache eviction for long reasoning generation) with a well-motivated empirical study identifying distinct attention patterns (global/positional/semantic-dependent) and the disproportionate loss increase on low-entropy tokens after eviction, which directly motivates the method design.

The two-stage training paradigm (supervised distillation from a principled 'Golden Eviction' oracle followed by GRPO-based RL that accounts for distribution shift during actual eviction-influenced decoding) is a sensible and reasonably novel combination not previously explored for KV eviction.

Extensive experimentation: three reasoning models, two AIME benchmarks with 32 repeated evaluations for statistical reliability, ablations on reward design, sampling strategy, and input features, plus a very large appendix covering scalability to 14B/32B models, additional baselines (G-KV, DuoAttention, RPC), cross-domain generalization (GPQA, LiveCodeBench, LongBench), length transfer, and throughput/latency analysis.
Clear efficiency gains are demonstrated (up to ~9.79x throughput improvement at low budgets) with negligible overhead from the scoring model itself (~2.7% of total generation time).
Attempted theoretical justification (Appendix A) connecting the Golden Eviction surrogate to bounds on attention-output/loss perturbation, adding some principled grounding beyond pure heuristics.
weaknesses: The closest prior training-based baseline explicitly discussed in the introduction and related work (Lancucki et al., 2025) is never empirically compared against in any experiment, leaving the core claimed advantage over other 'one-time judgment' trainable eviction methods unverified.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix A relies on several loose/strong assumptions (bounded value norms, local Lipschitzness of the logit and loss mappings, a multiplicative factor Ht that can be large) and mainly justifies the block-level surrogate used for label construction rather than the actual learned scoring model or the RL-refined policy, so its practical guarantees are limited.

The reward design (MSE loss on low-entropy, high-loss-increase tokens with a fixed margin η=1.5 and 80% threshold) appears to require nontrivial manual tuning; while some sensitivity analysis is provided in the appendix, the choices seem empirically selected rather than principled, raising concerns about robustness to new domains or models without re-tuning.

The scoring model's input features (multiple attention window sizes, decayed cumulative sums, raw key/value concatenation) add considerable engineering complexity and hyperparameters, which may hinder reproducibility and easy adaptation to different architectures (e.g., differing GQA group sizes, hidden dimensions).

Evaluation is centered on AIME2024/2025, which are small benchmarks (30 problems each); although pass@1 is averaged over 32 runs, the primary comparisons and most ablations rely on this narrow, math-specific evaluation before appendix generalization experiments are added.

No explicit discussion of limitations or failure modes of the method (e.g., cases where the scoring model or RL training might fail, sensitivity to distillation data quality/domain, memory/compute cost of training the scoring models across all layers and heads) is provided in the main text, and the Impact Statement is essentially a boilerplate placeholder.
